newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey says 1997 budget to remove IMF concerns.
newsitem.headline: Turkey says 1997 budget to remove IMF concerns.

text.p: Turkey's 1997 budget targeting a zero deficit should ward off concerns by the International Monetary Fund, which has said it will be difficult to achieve the targets, State Minister Ufuk Soylemez said on Thursday.

"Our (economic) practices in 1997 will succeed and it is highly likely they will be accepted by the IMF (International Monetary Fund)," he told parliamentary budget commission during the debate on the treasury's 1997 draft budget.
"Dialogue with the IMF will continue from the beginning of 1997. We feel that the IMF's proposals for solutions and those by us are gradually apporaching each other."
An IMF team visited Turkey in October to assess the economy and budget draft, and expressed reservations about the ambitious 1997 budgetary targets.
Soylemez did not say if Turkey would seek an IMF-backed medium-term stability programme through a stand-by accord with the IMF which is seen as vital by many economists and businessmen.
The IMF has repeatedly urged Turkey to implement a medium-term stabilisation programme including fiscal tightening, structural reforms and measures to break inflationary trends.
Turkey's 1997 draft budget proposes a zero deficit. It is expected to have 1,300 trillion lira budget deficit by end-1996.
"We believe the IMF's concerns will be removed after the implementation of budget and reform programmes in 1997", Soylemez said.
Soylemez also told the commission that Turkey's state economic enterprises were expected to make profits this year about nine times higher than those in 1995.
"KITs (state economic enterprises) are expected to turn over a total profit of 56.8 trillion lira in 1996. Their total profit was 6.3 trillion lira last year," he said.

He said the KITs were likely to more than double their profits to 127.6 trillion lira next year. Thee KITs will have been transferred a total capital of 48.5 trillion lira from the 1996 budget by the end of this year, up from 45.9 trillion lira in the previous year's budget, he said.
"Capital transfers to KITs are programmed at 92.4 trillion lira for 1997," he said.

Turkey set up the KITs decades ago to raise funds for the state, but their unwieldy management coupled with frequent abuses by politicians to raise their popularity among the electorate have caused many of them to be continuous loss making enterprises.
Turkey's 10-year-old, slow privatisation plan aims to sell off money-spinning KITs and some of the loss-makers after their rehabilitation.

Soylemez said the government would continue to support inports including fertilisers used in agriculture in 1997. Such supports will reach 100 trillion lira of budget spending in 1997, up from 43 trillion this year.

He also said Turkey's cash-strapped social security institutions, one of the major black holes draining state funds, would be given 530 trillion from the 1997 budget compared to 340 trillion lira this year.
He said some real estate belonging to these institutions would be sold off in 1997 to raise about 100 trillion lira to help their funding.
